A wrong answer like \( [-3.8] = -3 \) reveals the common misconception that the greatest integer function truncates toward zero (like computer integer division) instead of rounding down to the next lower integer.

questions.q: Explain why the graph of \( y = [x] \) has a closed circle at the left end of each step and an open circle at the right end, while the graph of \( y = \text{sgn}(x) \) has an isolated point at \( (0,0) \) with open circles at \( (0,1) \) and \( (0,-1) \).
questions.a: For \( [x] \), the definition \( n \le x < n+1 \) means the value \( n \) is attained at \( x = n \) (closed circle) but not at \( x = n+1 \) (open circle). For \( \text{sgn}(x) \), the three branches \( x<0 \), \( x=0 \), \( x>0 \) are mutually exclusive; at \( x=0 \) the value is exactly 0, while the limits from left and right are -1 and +1 respectively, so those limit points are not attained (open circles). A student who draws closed circles at both ends of a step for \( [x] \) misunderstands the half-open interval nature of the definition.

Step 1: By definition, \( [2x-1] = 3 \iff 3 \le 2x-1 < 4 \). Step 2: Add 1: \( 4 \le 2x < 5 \). Step 3: Divide by 2: \( 2 \le x < 2.5 \). Step 4: Solution set \( x \in [2, 2.5) \). A wrong answer \( x = 2 \) only shows the student treated \( [2x-1] = 3 \) as an equation \( 2x-1 = 3 \) instead of an inequality condition.

questions.q: Compare the solution sets of \( \text{sgn}(x^2 - 4) = 1 \) and \( [x^2 - 4] = 1 \). Are they the same? Justify.
questions.a: For \( \text{sgn}(x^2-4)=1 \), we need \( x^2-4 > 0 \Rightarrow x^2 > 4 \Rightarrow x < -2 \) or \( x > 2 \). For \( [x^2-4]=1 \), we need \( 1 \le x^2-4 < 2 \Rightarrow 5 \le x^2 < 6 \Rightarrow x \in [-\sqrt{6}, -\sqrt{5}] \cup [\sqrt{5}, \sqrt{6}] \). The sets are completely different: the first is two unbounded rays, the second is two bounded intervals. A student who says they are the same confuses the signum function (only cares about sign) with the greatest integer function (cares about magnitude intervals).

questions.q: A student claims that \( [x] + [-x] = 0 \) for all real \( x \). Is this correct? If not, give the correct identity and a counterexample.
questions.a:
The claim is false. Counterexample: \( x = 2.3 \Rightarrow [2.3] + [-2.3] = 2 + (-3) = -1 
eq 0 \). The correct identity is \( [x] + [-x] =  egin{cases} 0 & 	ext{if } x \in \mathbb{Z} \ -1 & 	ext{if } x 
otin \mathbb{Z} \end{cases} \). A student who agrees with the claim is likely thinking of the property \( 	ext{sgn}(x) + 	ext{sgn}(-x) = 0 \) (for \( x 
eq 0 \)) and incorrectly transferring it to the greatest integer function.

questions.q: Create a real-life problem (Indian context) that can be modelled using the greatest integer function, write the mathematical model, and solve it for a given input.
questions.a: Example: A Delhi Metro token costs ₹10 for the first 2 km and ₹5 for every additional km or part thereof. If a passenger travels 7.3 km, what is the fare? Model: Fare = \( 10 + 5 \times [\text{distance} - 2] \) for distance > 2 km. For 7.3 km: extra = \( [7.3 - 2] = [5.3] = 5 \) km. Fare = \( 10 + 5 \times 5 = ₹35 \). A poor answer uses \( \text{distance} - 2 = 5.3 \) directly (giving ₹36.5) ignoring the "part thereof" clause that requires the greatest integer function.
